words.etymon: (context line Beo. 3025) mapped pie-lex-sker; imitative *ḱor-/kor-, cf. Lat coruus
(context line s21) unmapped; compound of śvan- < *ḱwṓ

cognate: *ḱwṓ 'dog' (Lat canes; AV śvā-pada; Gk κύνες in Homer support; Ved śvan in AVŚ 11.2.2) and *wĺ̥kʷos 'wolf' (OE wulf; Lat lupi) as the ground-beast member; *h₂ewi- 'bird' (Gk οἰωνοί, Ved vayāṃsi in AVŚ 11.2.2) as the bird member in Greek and Vedic. So the Greek and Vedic binomial 'dogs and birds' has both members cognate.
drift_or_renewal: The bird member is renewed outside Greek/Vedic: hrefn/earn in OE, coruus/uulturius in Latin, gṛdhra/dhvāṅkṣa/śakuni in AV 11.9 next to vayas in AV 11.2. The dog member is renewed as wolf in Germanic (wulf; the dog is still there in ON tíkr, HHund I 46) and turns up in a compound in AV śvā-pada 'beast of prey'. The verb for gorging is renewed in each branch: Ved tṛp- 'be sated' (cognate with Gk τέρπω, not with the Homeric word), Gk κορέννυμι, ON seðja, OE æt ǣte spōwan / ǣses brūcan, Lat uorare.
shared_syntax: Dative/locative of the scavengers with a verb of making, giving or sating, and the enemy's corpse or flesh as the meal: Gk ἑλώρια τεῦχε κύνεσσιν οἰωνοῖσί τε 'made them prey for dogs and birds' ~ Ved śune ... mā śarīrāṇi kartam 'do not make (our) bodies for the dog' (AVŚ 11.2.2). Causative or intransitive 'be sated' with the scavengers as subject and the enemy as locus: AV tṛpyantu amitreṣu 'let them be sated on the enemies' ~ Gk κορέει κύνας ἠδ' οἰωνούς 'he will glut the dogs and birds' ~ ON hrafna seðja á hræum 'sate the ravens on corpses'. In the OE and Latin anchors the scavengers are paired ground beast + carrion bird (wulf + hrefn/earn; canes/lupi + coruus/uulturius).
context: Every anchor sits in the same context: the unburied dead of battle, or of a curse, as food for scavengers. Beowulf 3024-3028 has the messenger foretelling the raven telling the eagle how he fared at the feast while he and the wolf plundered the slain. Catullus 108.3-6 is a curse in which tongue, eyes, guts and limbs go to vulture, raven, dogs and wolves. AVŚ 11.9.19-22 is a battle charm in which vultures, hawks, crows and birds are to be sated on the enemies, and every beast of prey on the human corpse. Antigone 27-30 has Polyneices left unwept and unburied, a sweet store for birds. The Homeric support (Il. 1.4-5 and the 'glut dogs and birds' line) is the classic epic statement of the same theme.
phrase: '(make) the slain (into) a meal for dogs/wolves and birds' / 'sate the scavengers on the enemy's corpse' (Gk κύνεσσιν οἰωνοῖσί τε; Ved śune ... vayāṃsi; OE wulf ... hrefn ... earn; Lat canes ... lupi ... coruus)
note: The motif is naturalistic, and any warrior tradition could invent scavengers. The case for inheritance rests on three things: the doubly cognate Greek~Vedic binomial (*ḱwon- + *h₂ewi-), the same 'make bodies for the dog' / 'sate on the enemy' constructions, and the motif being formulaic in Homer, the AV, OE and the Edda. The Greek and Vedic binomial itself is attested only in support (Homer, AVŚ 11.2.2), not in this slab's passage lines; the slab anchors give the motif plus the dog/wolf cognates. Several key words (canes, lupi, hrefn, śvāpada, οἰωνοῖς) sit in the anchors' context lines rather than in the passage lines. The comparison of the 'beasts of battle' / 'food for dogs and birds' theme across IE traditions is recalled from the literature (e.g. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth).

Read all 272 bundles; one claim (beasts of battle / food for dogs and birds, medium). Partners are mostly mapping noise (Cato Agr., Aristotle, Hippocrates, ORV chronicles against OE poetry). Weighed and rejected: OE forst and sniw ~ Lucr. nix/pruina (Azarias renders the Benedicite pruinae et nives, so a calque); OE niht-longne ~ Lat. nox longa (generic); OE swēg ~ Gk ἰαχή (no shared collocation); OE word ... cwæð ~ ON orð ... kvað (single branch).
